name: Your vs you're -- the possessive-apostrophe punchline
scope: The single most-corrected error on the internet, taught by the misuse punchline. T1: someone writes 'Your the best' as a compliment -- the sentence literally means 'the best belongs to you' and never finishes. The rule: 'your' shows possession (your dog, your homework), 'you're' is a contraction of 'you are' with the missing 'a' marked by the apostrophe. T2: the swap test -- read the sentence with 'you are' out loud; if it still works, use 'you're'. 'Your going to school' becomes 'You are going to school' -- so 'you're'. T3: the reversed trap -- 'You're dog is chasing the mailman' fails the swap ('You are dog is chasing the mailman') so it must be 'your'. T4: the tricky combo -- 'You're right about your homework' has both, and the swap test confirms each one. T5: the register note -- 'ur' in texting is a third thing entirely (very informal); it's not a rule violation, it's a register choice, and it doesn't belong in an essay.
source: Grokipedia 'Your and you're' entry (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster usage note 'your' vs 'you're'; Chicago Manual of Style 17e 5.220-5.221 (contractions with apostrophe for elision). CORROBORATE AT BUILD: MW usage note wording; CMOS section numbers.
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (the compliment that literally never finishes). Kid catches an adult writing 'your welcome' on a card. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem QUOTES the wrong sentence, answer names the rule or gives the fix -- never spell out 'this is missing a contraction' before asking. SCENE = the quoted misuse (birthday card, text message, homework note). DISTRACTOR MINE: other apostrophe confusables as rule names (its/it's, there/their/they're, whose/who's, lets/let's) so a careful kid picks the specific 'your vs you're' rule and not a general 'apostrophe missing'. CHOICE PARITY: if answer is a corrected sentence, all four are corrected/miscorrected sentences of similar length; if answer is a rule name, all four are real grammar-rule names. KID-SAFE: pets, cards, texts, homework.

name: There, their, they're -- the three-way apostrophe trap
scope: Three words, one sound, three completely different jobs. T1: 'Their going to there house with they're dog' -- all three are wrong. 'There' points to a place (over THERE), 'their' shows possession (THEIR dog), 'they're' is the contraction of 'they are' (THEY'RE going). T2: the memory trick -- 'there' has 'here' inside it (both are places); 'their' has 'heir' inside it (an heir INHERITS -- possession); 'they're' has the apostrophe marking the missing 'a' from 'are'. T3: the swap test for 'they're' -- read 'they are' out loud in place of it; if it still works, use 'they're'. T4: the tricky combo -- 'They're going to their house over there' uses all three correctly and each passes its own test. T5: the plural-possessive edge -- 'their' works for one person too in modern English (singular they has been standard since Shakespeare); 'somebody left their coat' is fine, not a rule violation.
source: Grokipedia 'There, their, they're' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster usage note on 'there/their/they're' and the singular-they entry; Chicago Manual of Style 17e 5.48 (singular they accepted). CORROBORATE AT BUILD: MW singular-they usage note wording.
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (an all-three-wrong sentence). Kid catches a text message using the wrong one. T5 crosses into a LIGHTLY prescriptive-vs-descriptive judgment (singular they) -- mark that rung `vision_mandated: true` at build if it invokes the debate as a payoff; if it just states the modern consensus as a passing note, leave it neutral. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem QUOTES the misuse. DISTRACTOR MINE: your/you're, its/it's, whose/who's as adjacent rule-name distractors. CHOICE PARITY enforced. KID-SAFE.

name: Its vs it's -- the one apostrophe that flips the meaning
scope: The exception that trips up almost everyone. T1: 'The dog wagged it's tail' -- looks right, is wrong. 'It's' with the apostrophe ALWAYS means 'it is' or 'it has'; 'its' without the apostrophe is the possessive (like his, hers, ours -- none of those take an apostrophe either). T2: WHY it's backwards from every other possessive -- normally 's' shows possession (the dog's tail). But the possessive pronouns (his, hers, its, ours, theirs) NEVER take apostrophes; the apostrophe on 'it's' is reserved for the contraction. T3: the swap test -- read 'it is' out loud in place. 'It's raining' becomes 'It is raining' -- correct. 'The tree lost it's leaves' becomes 'The tree lost it is leaves' -- broken, so it must be 'its'. T4: the end-of-sentence edge -- 'The book is on its side' (possessive, no apostrophe); 'The book is on its side, isn't it?' (still possessive at 'its'). T5: the double-check -- if you can substitute 'his' or 'her' and the sentence still makes sense, you want the no-apostrophe 'its'. 'The dog wagged HIS tail' works, so 'The dog wagged its tail' -- no apostrophe.
source: Grokipedia 'It's vs its' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster 'its' and 'it's' entries; Chicago Manual of Style 17e 5.50 (possessive pronouns take no apostrophe), 5.220 (contractions). CORROBORATE AT BUILD: CMOS 5.50 wording.
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the whole 's-for-possession' pattern REVERSES for pronouns -- that's the WHY). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the misuse. DISTRACTOR MINE: whose/who's (parallel possessive-pronoun exception), your/you're, hers/her's (her's is ALWAYS wrong). CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE: pets, books, weather.

name: To, too, two -- three tiny words, three jobs
scope: The commonest three-way homophone in English. T1: 'I want too pieces of cake to' -- wrong twice. 'To' is a preposition or the infinitive marker (go TO the store, I want TO cake); 'too' means 'also' or 'excessively' (me TOO, TOO much); 'two' is the number 2. T2: the memory trick -- 'too' has an EXTRA 'o' because it means 'in excess' or 'in addition'; think of it as the extra letter for the extra meaning. T3: the swap tests -- if you can say 'also' or 'excessively' in its place, use 'too'; if you can substitute the digit '2', use 'two'; otherwise use 'to'. T4: the triple sentence -- 'I ate two cookies, and I want to eat one more too' uses all three correctly. T5: the edge case -- 'too' at the end of a sentence sometimes takes a comma before it for emphasis ('I want one, too'), sometimes not ('I want one too') -- both are acceptable; the comma just adds a beat of pause.
source: Grokipedia 'To, too, two' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster 'to', 'too', 'two' entries; Chicago Manual of Style 17e 6.29 (comma before 'too' -- optional, for emphasis). CORROBORATE AT BUILD: CMOS 6.29 wording.
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the extra 'o' MEANS the extra meaning -- a memory trick that sticks). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the misuse. DISTRACTOR MINE: other homophone-triplets (there/their/they're, right/write/rite) as rule-name distractors. CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE: cookies, cake, homework.

name: Then vs than -- time vs comparison
scope: One letter, one enormous difference. T1: 'She is taller then her brother' -- wrong. 'Then' is about TIME or SEQUENCE (first this, THEN that; back THEN); 'than' is used in COMPARISONS (taller THAN, more THAN, better THAN). T2: the memory trick -- 'thEn' has an 'e' like 'timE' or 'sEquence'; 'thAn' has an 'a' like 'compAre' or 'contrAst'. T3: the swap test -- if the sentence is comparing two things, use 'than'. 'I would rather eat pizza than salad' compares pizza and salad -- 'than'. 'I ate pizza, then went to bed' orders events in time -- 'then'. T4: the tricky pair -- 'She is taller than her brother, and then he grew' uses both correctly. T5: the register note -- 'different than' vs 'different from' is a live style question; American English accepts 'different than' before a clause ('different than I remembered'); British English prefers 'different from' throughout. Neither is a mistake, just a regional preference.
source: Grokipedia 'Then vs than' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster usage notes on 'than' and 'different from/than'; Chicago Manual of Style 17e 5.185 ('different from' preferred, 'different than' accepted before clauses). CORROBORATE AT BUILD: CMOS 5.185 wording.
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the E-for-time / A-for-comparison mnemonic). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the misuse. DISTRACTOR MINE: other one-letter-flip pairs (lose/loose, quiet/quite) as adjacent traps. CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE: pizza, siblings, bedtime.

name: Lose vs loose -- one O or two
scope: The one-letter mistake that changes the whole sentence. T1: 'Don't loose your homework!' -- wrong. 'Lose' (one O) is a VERB meaning to misplace something or to fail to win (I lose, you lose, we all LOSE); 'loose' (two Os) is an ADJECTIVE meaning not tight (LOOSE tooth, LOOSE change, LOOSE screw). T2: the memory trick -- 'loose' has TWO Os because it's LOOSE (spread out); 'lose' has just one because when you LOSE something, you have LESS of it. T3: the swap tests -- if it means 'not tight' or 'not attached', use 'loose'. If it means 'misplace' or 'fail to win', use 'lose'. 'The team will LOSE the game' (fail to win) -- one O. 'The screw is LOOSE' (not tight) -- two Os. T4: the tricky combo -- 'If the screw is loose, you'll lose the wheel' uses both correctly. T5: the noun edge -- 'a loss' is the noun form of 'lose' (I took a LOSS); 'to loosen' is the verb form of 'loose' (LOOSEN the belt). Different roots, different families.
source: Grokipedia 'Lose vs loose' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster 'lose' and 'loose' entries. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: MW etymology entries (different Old English roots).
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the 'LOOSE has two Os because it's LOOSE' mnemonic). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the misuse. DISTRACTOR MINE: chose/choose (parallel one-O/two-Os pair, but present/past-tense), then/than as adjacent one-letter-flip. CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE: teeth, screws, sports.

name: Affect vs effect -- verb vs noun (usually)
scope: The pair that even English teachers double-check. T1: 'The rain effected our picnic' -- wrong. In 99% of use: 'affect' is a VERB meaning 'to influence' (the rain AFFECTED our picnic); 'effect' is a NOUN meaning 'the result' (the EFFECT of the rain was a soggy blanket). T2: the memory trick -- RAVEN: Remember, Affect is a Verb, Effect is a Noun. T3: the swap tests -- if you can put 'the' in front, you want the noun 'effect' ('the effect was...'). If it's what something DOES to something else, you want the verb 'affect' ('the noise affects my sleep'). T4: THE 1% -- 'effect' CAN be a verb meaning 'to bring about' ('the new policy will EFFECT changes' = 'will cause changes to happen'); 'affect' CAN be a noun in psychology meaning 'displayed emotion' ('the patient had a flat AFFECT'). These are rare; teach the 99% rule first. T5: the tricky combo -- 'The cold weather affects the crops, and the effect is a smaller harvest' uses each in its common role.
source: Grokipedia 'Affect vs effect' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster 'affect' and 'effect' entries + usage notes; Chicago Manual of Style 17e 5.220 (affect/effect usage). CORROBORATE AT BUILD: MW usage note wording for the rare verb-effect / noun-affect uses.
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (RAVEN acronym). T4 is the specialist rung -- gives the honest edge cases without overwhelming the 99% rule. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the misuse. DISTRACTOR MINE: accept/except, assure/ensure/insure as adjacent verb-vs-noun / near-homophone traps. CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE: rain, picnics, sleep, weather.

name: Accept vs except -- take in vs leave out
scope: Two words with opposite meanings that sound almost the same. T1: 'Everyone came accept my brother' -- wrong. 'Accept' means to RECEIVE or agree to (I ACCEPT your apology); 'except' means to EXCLUDE or leave out (everyone came EXCEPT my brother). T2: the memory trick -- accEpt starts with 'ac-' like 'ACquire' (get, take in); Except starts with 'ex-' like 'EXclude' or 'EXit' (out, away). T3: the swap tests -- if you can substitute 'take' or 'agree to', use 'accept'. If you can substitute 'but not' or 'excluding', use 'except'. 'I accept the gift' (take it); 'everyone except me' (excluding me). T4: the tricky combo -- 'I will accept every apology except a sarcastic one' uses both correctly. T5: the register note -- 'except that' can start a clause ('I would have gone, except that I was sick'), which is where speakers accidentally reach for 'accept'; the clue is that 'except that' means 'but' -- a subtractor, not an accepter.
source: Grokipedia 'Accept vs except' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster 'accept' and 'except' entries + usage notes.
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (ac- for acquire, ex- for exclude). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the misuse. DISTRACTOR MINE: affect/effect, adverse/averse as adjacent near-homophones. CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE: parties, apologies, siblings.

name: Principal vs principle -- the person, the money, the rule
scope: One is a person you know from school, one is a rule you live by. T1: 'The principal of the story is: don't lie' -- wrong. 'Principal' (with -pal) is the head of a school, or a main/most-important thing, or the original sum of money in a loan; 'principle' (with -ple) is a RULE, standard, or belief. T2: the memory trick -- your PrincipAL is your PAL (the person); a PrinciPLE is a ruLE. T3: the swap tests -- if you can say 'the head' or 'the main one', use 'principal' (the PRINCIPAL reason = the main reason). If you can say 'the rule' or 'the belief', use 'principle' (a matter of PRINCIPLE = a matter of belief). T4: the money meaning -- when you take out a loan, the PRINCIPAL is the original amount borrowed (before interest); the interest is calculated on the principal. Still spelled with -pal because it's the 'main' amount. T5: the tricky combo -- 'The principal of our school teaches us the principle of honesty' uses both correctly, one as a person and one as a rule.
source: Grokipedia 'Principal vs principle' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster 'principal' and 'principle' entries + usage notes.
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (principAL is your PAL). T4 is the finance-vocab rung -- teaches a useful money term along the way. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the misuse. DISTRACTOR MINE: capital/capitol, complement/compliment, stationary/stationery (parallel -al/-le or -al/-ol pairs). CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE: school, honesty, savings accounts.

name: Stationary vs stationery -- standing still vs writing paper
scope: One little letter, one enormous difference. T1: 'I bought some stationary for my thank-you cards' -- wrong. 'Stationary' (with -ary) means NOT MOVING (a stationary bicycle at the gym); 'stationery' (with -ery) means writing PAPER, envelopes, and pens. T2: the memory trick -- stationERy has an E, like Envelope or lEtter (writing supplies); stationARy has an A, like stAy or stAnd (not moving). T3: the swap tests -- if you can say 'still' or 'not moving', use 'stationary' (a stationary car = a still car). If you can say 'paper' or 'writing supplies', use 'stationery'. T4: the etymology tag -- both come from 'station' because in medieval England, most merchants moved from town to town, but the sellers of paper and books had fixed STATIONS -- so their goods became STATIONERY, spelled with an E to mark the paper-shop meaning. T5: the tricky combo -- 'The stationery is in the drawer of the stationary desk' uses both correctly and each is spelled to fit its meaning.
source: Grokipedia 'Stationary and stationery' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster 'stationary' and 'stationery' entries; Oxford English Dictionary etymology for 'stationer' (medieval stationarii, booksellers with fixed shops). CORROBORATE AT BUILD: OED etymology wording.
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (E for envelope, A for stay). T4 is a genuine etymology rung -- the two spellings SPLIT for a real historical reason. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the misuse. DISTRACTOR MINE: complement/compliment, principal/principle (parallel -e/-a spelling flips). CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE: gyms, letters, desks.

name: Complement vs compliment -- completing vs praising
scope: One completes, the other praises. T1: 'Her scarf really compliments her jacket' -- wrong. 'Complement' (with -e-) means to COMPLETE or go well WITH something (the scarf COMPLEMENTS the jacket = it completes the outfit); 'compliment' (with -i-) is a spoken PRAISE ('nice scarf!' is a COMPLIMENT). T2: the memory trick -- comPLEment shares its -PLE- with comPLEte; comPLIment shares its -I- with 'I like it!' (a praise from ME). T3: the swap tests -- if you can substitute 'complete' or 'go well with', use 'complement'. If you can substitute 'praise', use 'compliment'. 'The wine complemented the meal' (completed) vs 'She complimented the chef' (praised). T4: the noun 'a complement' -- in grammar it's the word that COMPLETES a sentence's meaning ('she is a TEACHER' -- 'teacher' is the complement of 'is'); in math, complementary angles ADD UP TO 90 degrees (they complete a right angle). T5: the tricky combo -- 'She complimented me on how the necklace complements my dress' uses both correctly.
source: Grokipedia 'Complement vs compliment' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster 'complement' and 'compliment' entries + usage notes; Chicago Manual of Style 17e 5.220 (usage guide).
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (comPLEte / comPLImentI mnemonic). T4 shows the noun serves in both grammar (sentence-complement) and math (complementary angles) -- cross-subject usefulness. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the misuse. DISTRACTOR MINE: principal/principle, stationary/stationery. CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE: clothes, meals, math class.

name: Capital vs capitol -- the city, the money, the building
scope: Same sound, one meaning is a building. T1: 'The state capitol is Sacramento' -- wrong. 'Capital' (with -al) covers almost every meaning: the CAPITAL city, CAPITAL letters, CAPITAL punishment, financial CAPITAL. 'Capitol' (with -ol) is used only for one thing: the actual BUILDING where a legislature meets. T2: the memory trick -- capitOl has an O like the dOme on a capitol building. Every other meaning gets the -al spelling. T3: the swap tests -- if you're naming a city (Paris is the CAPITAL of France), a letter (a CAPITAL A), or money (start-up CAPITAL) -- use 'capital'. If you're pointing at the specific BUILDING where lawmakers meet -- use 'capitol'. T4: the etymology -- 'capitol' comes from the Capitoline Hill in ancient Rome, one of the seven hills, where the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus stood. Every American state capitol echoes that Roman word for its lawmaking hall. T5: the tricky combo -- 'The capital of Texas is Austin, and the state capitol building has a pink granite dome' uses both correctly.
source: Grokipedia 'Capital vs capitol' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster 'capital' and 'capitol' entries; Chicago Manual of Style 17e 8.63 (Capitol -- U.S. Capitol capitalization).
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (capitOl has an O like the dOme). T4 gives real etymology (Capitoline Hill) -- a small history-hook that anchors the spelling. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the misuse. DISTRACTOR MINE: principal/principle, complement/compliment. CHOICE PARITY. APOLITICAL: use state capitols (Sacramento, Austin) not current national politics; historical (Roman Capitoline Hill) is safe.

name: Whose vs who's -- the possessive pronoun exception, again
scope: Same trap as its/it's, one letter different. T1: 'Who's coat is this?' -- wrong. 'Who's' (with the apostrophe) means 'who is' or 'who has' (WHO'S coming to dinner? = who is coming?). 'Whose' (no apostrophe) shows possession (WHOSE coat is this? = to whom does this coat belong?). T2: WHY it works this way -- like its/it's, the possessive pronoun 'whose' takes NO apostrophe (just like his, hers, ours, theirs). The apostrophe on 'who's' is saved for the contraction. T3: the swap test -- read 'who is' out loud in place. 'Who's at the door?' becomes 'Who is at the door?' -- correct. 'Who's coat is this?' becomes 'Who is coat is this?' -- broken; must be 'whose'. T4: the double-check -- if you can substitute 'his' or 'her' and it still makes sense as a possessive, use 'whose'. 'Whose book is it?' -- try 'his book' -- works, so 'whose'. T5: the tricky combo -- 'Who's the person whose coat this is?' uses both correctly and each passes its own test.
source: Grokipedia 'Whose vs who's' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster 'whose' and 'who's' entries; Chicago Manual of Style 17e 5.50 (possessive pronouns take no apostrophe).
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (same pattern as its/it's -- possessive pronouns REFUSE the apostrophe). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the misuse. DISTRACTOR MINE: its/it's (parallel rule), your/you're, there/their/they're. CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE: coats, doors, guests.

name: Less vs fewer -- mass vs count
scope: The rule the supermarket express lane got wrong. T1: '10 items or less' -- traditionally, this sign should read '10 items or FEWER'. 'Fewer' is for things you can COUNT ONE-BY-ONE (fewer cookies, fewer people, fewer books); 'less' is for things you measure as a MASS (less water, less time, less money). T2: the memory trick -- if you can put a NUMBER in front of it (three cookies, five books), use 'fewer'. If you can't naturally put a number in front (three waters? three sands? -- no), use 'less'. T3: the swap tests -- 'less water in the pool' (measured, can't count drops) vs 'fewer swimmers in the pool' (each one is a distinct person). T4: the exceptions the rule ALLOWS -- for measurements of time, money, and distance treated as a single amount, 'less' is correct even though they're technically countable: 'less than five miles', 'less than ten dollars', 'less than an hour'. Nobody says 'fewer than five miles'. T5: the usage note -- 'less' has been used for countable things in English since around 900 AD (King Alfred used it that way); the 'less/fewer' rule was invented in 1770 by a grammarian named Robert Baker. It's a real style rule to follow, but not an ancient one. Mark rung `vision_mandated: true` if invoking the descriptivist point.
source: Grokipedia 'Fewer vs less' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster usage note on 'less' vs 'fewer' + the 1770 Robert Baker origin; Chicago Manual of Style 17e 5.250 (less vs fewer).
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (this 'rule' is only 250 years old; even Alfred the Great broke it). T5 crosses into descriptivist-vs-prescriptivist -- mark that rung `vision_mandated: true` at build if it takes a considered position. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the misuse. DISTRACTOR MINE: much/many (same rule for adjectives), amount/number (same rule for nouns). CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE: supermarkets, pools, cookies.

name: Who vs whom -- the M means object
scope: The rule your grandparents insist on, plus the honest modern usage note. T1: 'Who did you invite?' vs 'Whom did you invite?' -- both are heard; formally, 'whom' is correct because he/she/they is being INVITED (object). 'Who' is the SUBJECT form (WHO is coming? = HE is coming); 'whom' is the OBJECT form (WHOM did you invite? = you invited HIM). T2: the memory trick -- try substituting HE or HIM. If HE works, use WHO. If HIM works, use WHOM. Both 'him' and 'whom' end in -M. 'Who called?' -- 'He called' -- who. 'Whom did you call?' -- 'You called him' -- whom. T3: the tricky preposition case -- after a preposition, formally always use 'whom': 'to WHOM it may concern', 'for WHOM the bell tolls', 'with WHOM did you go?'. In casual speech people say 'who did you go with?' and it's understood. T4: the trap -- 'Give it to whoever wants it' -- looks like it should be 'whomever' after the preposition 'to', but 'whoever wants it' is a whole clause where 'whoever' is the SUBJECT of 'wants'; so 'whoever' is correct. T5: the register note -- 'whom' is fading in casual speech and everyday writing; most style guides now say it's fine to use 'who' when 'whom' would sound stiff, and to use 'whom' in formal writing (business letters, academic papers). Neither is wrong; register is the choice. Mark rung `vision_mandated: true` if invoking the prescriptivist-vs-descriptivist framing.
source: Grokipedia 'Who vs whom' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster 'who' and 'whom' usage note; Chicago Manual of Style 17e 5.66-5.67 (relative pronouns, who/whom); Garner's Modern English Usage 4e 'whom' entry.
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE / register-clarity. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the HE/HIM swap test -- both end in -M). T5 crosses into descriptivist territory -- mark that rung `vision_mandated: true`. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the sentence, answer names the form. DISTRACTOR MINE: I/me (same subject/object rule), we/us. CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE: invitations, phone calls.

name: That vs which -- restrictive vs non-restrictive
scope: The comma rule that changes what a sentence MEANS. T1: 'The bike that is red is mine' vs 'The bike, which is red, is mine' -- BOTH are correct English, but they mean different things. 'That' introduces a RESTRICTIVE clause (which bike? the red one, not the blue one -- essential info); 'which' with commas introduces a NON-RESTRICTIVE clause (there's only one bike; by the way, it's red -- extra info). T2: the memory trick -- if you can put COMMAS around the clause AND remove it without changing the sentence's core meaning, use 'which'. If removing it loses essential info, use 'that' with no commas. T3: the swap test -- 'The cars that are speeding will be ticketed' (only the speeding cars, not all cars) vs 'The cars, which are speeding, will be ticketed' (all the cars, and by the way they're all speeding). Same words, different meaning. T4: the tricky combo -- 'The dog that barks loudest belongs to my neighbor' (identifying WHICH dog) vs 'My neighbor's dog, which barks loudest, is a beagle' (there's just one dog, extra info). T5: the register note -- this rule is stronger in American English than British; British writers often use 'which' for both. American style guides (Chicago, AP) strongly prefer the that/which split. Mark rung `vision_mandated: true` if invoking the prescriptivist choice.
source: Grokipedia 'That vs which' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster usage note on 'that' vs 'which'; Chicago Manual of Style 17e 6.27 (restrictive vs non-restrictive clauses), 5.250 ('that' vs 'which'); AP Stylebook 'that, which' entry.
framing_note: REGISTER / CLARITY CONTRAST -- two grammatically valid sentences, one says exactly what you mean. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (the commas literally change what the sentence CLAIMS). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the pair, answer names the meaning-difference. Companion rule: introduces the vocab (restrictive / non-restrictive) with example sentences per the vocab-teaching invariant. DISTRACTOR MINE: who vs whom, singular they. CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE: bikes, cars, dogs.

name: Imply vs infer -- speaker vs listener
scope: One is what the SPEAKER does, one is what the LISTENER does. T1: 'Are you inferring that I'm lying?' -- wrong. 'Imply' is what the SPEAKER does (to hint at something without saying it directly); 'infer' is what the LISTENER does (to figure out what wasn't said directly). If someone hints at something, THEY imply, YOU infer. T2: the memory trick -- IMPLY starts with I like 'I hint' (the speaker); INFER starts with 'IN' like 'INcoming information' (the listener taking it IN). T3: the swap test -- who is doing the action? 'The teacher IMPLIED that homework would be graded' (the teacher hinted) vs 'The students INFERRED that homework would be graded' (the students figured out from the hint). T4: the tricky combo -- 'The teacher implied there would be a quiz, and we inferred we should study' uses both correctly, one per party. T5: the historical note -- 'infer' HAS been used to mean 'imply' since the 1500s (John Milton did it); but modern style guides and formal writing keep the distinction because the two-word pair is genuinely useful.
source: Grokipedia 'Imply vs infer' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster usage note on 'infer' + the Milton citation; Chicago Manual of Style 17e 5.250 (imply/infer).
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (I-for-'I hint' / IN-for-incoming). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the misuse. DISTRACTOR MINE: assure/ensure/insure (three-way close-cousin), teach/learn (parallel speaker/listener pair -- often misused). CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE: teachers, students, quizzes.

name: Farther vs further -- physical distance vs figurative
scope: One measures miles, the other measures ideas. T1: 'Let's discuss this farther' -- traditionally wrong. 'Farther' is for PHYSICAL distance you can measure (how much FARTHER to the beach?); 'further' is for FIGURATIVE or ADDITIONAL amounts (look FURTHER into the matter; go FURTHER in your career). T2: the memory trick -- FARther has FAR inside it, and FAR is a distance you can walk; FURther is used for FURthering an idea or going FURther in a discussion. T3: the swap tests -- if you can substitute 'more miles' or 'a longer distance', use 'farther'. If you can substitute 'more' or 'additional', use 'further'. 'Two miles farther down the road' (distance) vs 'nothing further to add' (additional info). T4: the note about 'furthermore' -- 'furthermore' (never 'farthermore') is always figurative; it means 'in addition' and is standard for adding a new point to an argument. T5: the honest usage note -- most modern speakers use 'further' for both meanings; 'farther' is fading. Both are correct in most style guides today, but formal writing still respects the split. Mark rung `vision_mandated: true` if invoking the prescriptivist choice.
source: Grokipedia 'Farther vs further' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster usage note on 'farther' and 'further'; Chicago Manual of Style 17e 5.250 (farther/further).
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE / usage-register. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (FARther has FAR inside). T5 crosses into descriptivist territory -- mark that rung `vision_mandated: true` if it invokes the debate. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the misuse. DISTRACTOR MINE: less/fewer (parallel physical-vs-abstract), then/than. CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE: road trips, career, homework.

name: i.e. vs e.g. -- 'that is' vs 'for example'
scope: Two Latin abbreviations, two different jobs. T1: 'I love citrus fruits, i.e. oranges and lemons' -- often wrong. 'i.e.' means 'that is' (in other words, a full restatement) -- so this sentence claims citrus fruits ARE only oranges and lemons. To give EXAMPLES from a larger set, use 'e.g.' meaning 'for example'. T2: the memory trick -- I.E. = 'In Essence' (a restatement); E.G. = 'Example Given' (one of many). T3: the swap tests -- if you can substitute 'in other words' or 'specifically', use 'i.e.' If you can substitute 'for example' or 'such as', use 'e.g.' 'Only mammals (i.e. animals that nurse their young)' -- the parenthetical DEFINES mammals. 'Some mammals (e.g. dogs, cats, whales)' -- the parenthetical LISTS examples. T4: the style note -- both take periods after each letter and (in American style) a comma after the whole abbreviation: 'i.e., in other words'. Chicago and AP both keep the periods. T5: the etymology -- 'i.e.' is from Latin ID EST ('that is'); 'e.g.' is from Latin EXEMPLI GRATIA ('for the sake of example'). Both entered English in the 17th century. Some style guides now recommend replacing them with the English 'that is' and 'for example' for clarity.
source: Grokipedia 'i.e. vs e.g.' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster 'i.e.' and 'e.g.' entries + etymology; Chicago Manual of Style 17e 5.250 (i.e./e.g.), 6.44 (comma after i.e./e.g.); AP Stylebook.
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (I.E. = In Essence, E.G. = Example Given). T5 gives etymology (Latin origins). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the misuse. DISTRACTOR MINE: etc. (et cetera -- 'and the rest'), viz. (namely). CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE: fruits, animals, general examples.

name: Ensure, insure, assure -- three verbs, three targets
scope: Three near-homophones with three sharply different jobs. T1: 'I want to insure you that everything is fine' -- wrong. 'Assure' means to reassure a PERSON (I ASSURE you it's fine); 'ensure' means to make CERTAIN of an outcome (ENSURE the door is locked); 'insure' means to buy INSURANCE (INSURE your car against theft). T2: the memory trick -- ASSure has an S like 'reaSSure a perSon'; ENSure means 'make ENd-sure' (guarantee); INSure has 'IN-' like 'INcident' (things that go wrong, requiring insurance). T3: the swap tests -- if the object is a PERSON, use 'assure' (I assure YOU). If the object is a THING or OUTCOME, use 'ensure' (ensure the DOOR is locked). If money and a policy are involved, use 'insure' (insure your CAR). T4: the tricky combo -- 'I assure you the company insures its vehicles to ensure quick reimbursement' uses all three correctly. T5: the British/American note -- British English uses 'assure' more broadly, including for insurance products ('life assurance' in Britain = 'life insurance' in the US). Both are correct in their region.
source: Grokipedia 'Assure ensure insure' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster usage notes on 'assure', 'ensure', 'insure'; Chicago Manual of Style 17e 5.250 (assure/ensure/insure); Garner's Modern English Usage 4e.
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (mnemonic for each). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the misuse. DISTRACTOR MINE: affect/effect (parallel three-way if verb-effect counted), imply/infer. CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE: doors, cars, general reassurance.

name: Should of / could of / would of -- the impossible verb
scope: The eggcorn that makes English teachers wince. T1: 'I should of studied harder' -- always wrong. 'Of' is a preposition; it cannot follow a modal verb like 'should', 'could', or 'would'. The correct phrase is 'should HAVE studied' (or the contraction 'should've'). T2: WHY the mistake happens -- 'should've' sounds almost identical to 'should of' when spoken; the ear hears 'of' and the writer hands writes it that way. It's a sound-based error, not a logic-based one. T3: the fix -- ALWAYS write 'should have', 'could have', 'would have' (or their contractions 'should've', 'could've', 'would've'). Test yourself by expanding: 'I should HAVE gone' -- makes sense. 'I should OF gone' -- 'of gone' isn't a verb phrase; broken. T4: the related mistakes -- 'must of' (should be 'must have'), 'might of' (should be 'might have'), 'ought to of' (should be 'ought to have'). All the same pattern: modal + 'of' is impossible. T5: the register note -- this is a written mistake, not a spoken one; nobody knows if you SAID 'should of' or 'should've' -- they sound the same. It only becomes visible when written down, which is why texting and social media made it more common (and more corrected).
source: Grokipedia 'Should of' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster usage note on 'should have' / 'should've'; Garner's Modern English Usage 4e 'should of' entry (listed as a solecism); Chicago Manual of Style 17e 5.220 (contractions).
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE (canonical eggcorn). Dinner-test payoff: T1 (this is ALWAYS wrong -- the kid can catch adults doing it in a text). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the misuse. DISTRACTOR MINE: 'a lot' vs 'alot' (alot is never a word), 'all right' vs 'alright' (both accepted now in casual writing). CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE: studying, decisions, everyday regrets.

name: Irregardless -- the double-negative that isn't a word (mostly)
scope: The most-mocked non-word in English, and the honest usage note. T1: 'Irregardless of what you say, I'm going' -- traditionally wrong. The correct word is REGARDLESS. 'Irregardless' has both a prefix 'ir-' meaning 'not' AND a suffix '-less' meaning 'without' -- so it's a double-negative that literally means 'not without regard', the opposite of what people using it mean. T2: WHERE it comes from -- it appears to be a blend of 'irrespective' + 'regardless'; the first citation in Merriam-Webster is from 1795. It's been around for over 200 years but has always been considered nonstandard. T3: the fix -- use 'regardless' (or 'irrespective' if you want variety); both mean 'without regard to' and both are fully standard. T4: the honest modern note -- Merriam-Webster's dictionary DOES list 'irregardless' as a word (marked 'nonstandard'), because it's used often enough to be documented. Dictionaries describe usage; they don't only prescribe it. But no formal style guide RECOMMENDS it. T5: the register call -- 'irregardless' is fine in casual speech among friends who won't blink; it's a mistake to make in a job application, an essay, or a business email, where it marks the writer as careless. This is a genuine descriptivist-vs-prescriptivist question -- mark rung `vision_mandated: true`.
source: Grokipedia 'Irregardless' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster 'irregardless' entry + extensive usage note (1795 first citation, 'nonstandard' label); Garner's Modern English Usage 4e 'irregardless' (Stage 2, widely shunned).
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE + descriptivist/prescriptivist. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (a word that literally means the OPPOSITE of what its users mean). T5 is the honest register call -- mark `vision_mandated: true` because grammar-bank stance IS 'teach the standard but note actual usage'. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the misuse. DISTRACTOR MINE: 'unloosen' (double-negative that DOES mean 'to loosen'), 'inflammable' (misleadingly means 'catches fire easily'). CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE.

name: For all intensive purposes -- the eggcorn that changes the phrase
scope: One of the most-cited eggcorns in English. T1: 'For all intensive purposes, the game is over' -- wrong. The correct phrase is 'For all INTENTS AND PURPOSES', meaning 'in every practical sense'. 'Intensive purposes' would mean something like 'purposes that are very concentrated' -- which makes no sense in context. T2: WHERE the mistake comes from -- 'intents and purposes' and 'intensive purposes' sound almost identical when spoken quickly; the ear hears 'intensive' (a common word) and the writer preserves that mis-hearing. This kind of mistake is called an EGGCORN, named after someone hearing 'acorn' as 'eggcorn'. T3: the correct origin -- 'to all intents, constructions, and purposes' was a legal phrase in English law dating to the 1500s; it was shortened to 'to all intents and purposes' and then 'for all intents and purposes'. It means, in law, 'in every applicable sense'. T4: OTHER famous eggcorns -- 'one in the same' (should be 'one AND the same'); 'nip it in the butt' (should be 'nip it in the BUD' -- as in a plant); 'a mute point' (should be 'a MOOT point' -- meaning debatable); 'you've got another thing coming' (originally 'another THINK coming' -- a joke shortening of 'you've got another think coming to you'). T5: teach the term -- an EGGCORN preserves the mis-hearing because it seems to make its own kind of sense (a POUND that eats a chunk of your paycheck sounds vaguely plausible). Eggcorns are studied by linguists as evidence of how learners fit new phrases into words they already know.
source: Grokipedia 'Eggcorn' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster 'eggcorn' entry (added 2010, coined by linguist Geoffrey Pullum in 2003 on Language Log); Language Log 'Eggcorn' archive at languagelog.ldc.upenn.edu; Grokipedia 'For all intents and purposes' entry. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: the 1500s legal-English origin of 'intents and purposes'.
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE (canonical eggcorn). Dinner-test payoff: T4 (a rapid-fire list of eggcorns the kid can spot). T5 teaches the term 'eggcorn' with etymology (Pullum 2003, added to MW 2010). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the misuse. DISTRACTOR MINE: mondegreens (misheard song lyrics -- adjacent phenomenon), malapropisms (using the wrong word entirely). CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE: sports, plants, everyday phrases.

name: Peaked, peeked, piqued -- three verbs, one sound
scope: One of the trickiest three-way homophones in English. T1: 'That story really peaked my interest' -- wrong. 'Peaked' means reached the highest point ('the mountain PEAKED at 14,000 feet'); 'peeked' means took a quick look ('she PEEKED through the curtains'); 'piqued' means aroused or provoked ('the story PIQUED my curiosity'). T2: the memory tricks -- PEAK has a peak (a triangle A in the middle); PEEK has two Es like two EYES peeking; PIQUE comes from French pique meaning a sharp point that PROVOKES. T3: the swap tests -- if you can substitute 'topped out' or 'reached the highest', use 'peaked'. If you can substitute 'took a quick look', use 'peeked'. If you can substitute 'stirred up' or 'aroused', use 'piqued'. T4: the correct phrase for interest -- always 'piqued my interest' or 'piqued my curiosity' (stirred it up, made me want more). 'Peaked my interest' is the most common misuse. T5: the origin -- 'pique' entered English in the 1600s from French; it originally meant a fit of resentment ('a fit of PIQUE' still means that). The 'arouse curiosity' meaning developed from the sense of 'sharply provoke'.
source: Grokipedia 'Peaked peeked piqued' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster 'peak', 'peek', 'pique' entries + usage notes; Garner's Modern English Usage 4e.
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (mnemonics for each). T4 highlights the specific common misuse (peaked my interest -- the internet's most-corrected). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the misuse. DISTRACTOR MINE: right/write/rite (three-way), pair/pear/pare. CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE: mountains, curtains, books.

name: Bare vs bear -- naked vs the animal
scope: One means naked, the other is an animal (or a verb). T1: 'I can't bare to watch' -- wrong. 'Bare' is an adjective meaning naked or uncovered (BARE feet, BARE walls, BARE minimum); 'bear' is either the animal (a grizzly BEAR) or a verb meaning to CARRY or ENDURE (BEAR the weight, BEAR the pain, BEAR arms). T2: the memory trick -- BARE has A like nAked; BEAR is the animal you can dRAW; both meanings of 'bear' (animal + carry) go together because it's the same word. T3: the swap tests -- if you can substitute 'naked' or 'uncovered' or 'nothing but', use 'bare' (BARE hands = naked hands; the BARE minimum = the smallest amount, nothing more). If you can substitute 'endure', 'carry', or 'give birth to', use 'bear' (I can't BEAR the noise; BEAR the load; a woman BEARS a child). T4: the tricky combo -- 'The bear had to bear the weight of the bare tree branch' uses each form correctly and each is spelled to fit its meaning. T5: the idiom warning -- 'to bear in mind' (remember), 'to bear witness' (testify), 'bear with me' (be patient with me) all use BEAR, not BARE. 'Bear with me' means 'endure me a moment'; 'bare with me' would mean... something quite different.
source: Grokipedia 'Bare vs bear' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster 'bare' and 'bear' entries; Chicago Manual of Style 17e 5.250 (bare/bear).
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (bear with me vs bare with me -- the funny reading). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the misuse. DISTRACTOR MINE: pair/pear/pare, hair/hare, wear/where/were. CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE: animals, patience.

name: Breath vs breathe -- noun vs verb
scope: One letter, one whole change in what the word does. T1: 'Take a deep breathe' -- wrong. 'Breath' (rhymes with 'death', no E on the end) is the NOUN (take a deep BREATH, hold your BREATH); 'breathe' (rhymes with 'seethe', has an E on the end) is the VERB (BREATHE in, BREATHE out). T2: the memory trick -- brEAthE has an E on the end BECAUSE it's a vErb; the extra E marks the action. Also: breathE ends in E like takE, makE, seizE -- other action verbs. T3: the swap tests -- if it's an action, use 'breathe' (I BREATHE deeply). If it's a thing being taken, held, or given, use 'breath' (a BREATH of fresh air). T4: the related pair -- 'wreath' (a ring of flowers, noun) vs 'wreathe' (to encircle, verb) works exactly the same way. 'Wreaths on the door'; 'clouds wreathe the mountain'. T5: the tricky combo -- 'Take a deep breath, then breathe out slowly' uses both correctly, each in its part of speech.
source: Grokipedia 'Breath vs breathe' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster 'breath' and 'breathe' entries; Chicago Manual of Style 17e 5.220 (usage).
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (extra E = vErb). T4 extends the pattern to wreath/wreathe (companion pair). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the misuse. DISTRACTOR MINE: bathe/bath (parallel noun/verb E-marker), teethe/teeth. CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE: yoga, exercise, doors.

name: Discreet vs discrete -- careful vs separate
scope: Two spellings, two totally different meanings. T1: 'The company keeps their customer information discrete' -- probably wrong. 'Discreet' (two Es together) means CAREFUL, private, tactful ('be DISCREET about the surprise party'); 'discrete' (E-T-E) means SEPARATE, distinct, individually distinguishable ('the machine has three DISCRETE parts'). T2: the memory trick -- discreEt keeps its two Es tucked together (like a secret being kept private); discretE keeps its Es SEPARATE, split by the T (like the meaning: separate). T3: the swap tests -- if you can substitute 'careful' or 'tactful' or 'private', use 'discreet' (a DISCREET whisper). If you can substitute 'separate' or 'distinct' or 'individually countable', use 'discrete' (DISCRETE mathematics deals with countable, separate things -- integers, not continuous curves). T4: the specialty use -- in math, statistics, and computer science, 'discrete' is standard: DISCRETE variables (like the number of students) vs CONTINUOUS variables (like height, which flows without gaps). Kids see this word in math class. T5: the tricky combo -- 'She was discreet about the discrete files stored on her computer' uses both correctly.
source: Grokipedia 'Discreet vs discrete' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster 'discreet' and 'discrete' entries + usage notes; Chicago Manual of Style 17e 5.250 (discreet/discrete).
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (visual mnemonic -- Es tucked together for private, Es separated for separate). T4 gives a real math-class use case. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the misuse. DISTRACTOR MINE: complement/compliment, principal/principle. CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE: surprise parties, math class, computers.

name: Historic vs historical -- important vs from-the-past
scope: Two words used interchangeably, actually distinct in careful writing. T1: 'The museum has many historic documents' -- often loose. Traditionally: 'historic' means IMPORTANT IN HISTORY, significant enough to be remembered (a HISTORIC victory, a HISTORIC building where something major happened); 'historical' means simply RELATING TO THE PAST or to history as a subject (HISTORICAL documents, HISTORICAL fiction, HISTORICAL research). T2: the memory trick -- HISTORIC = HISTORY-MAKING (a moment history remembers); HISTORICAL = HISTORY-RELATED (just from or about the past). T3: the swap tests -- if you can substitute 'famous' or 'landmark' or 'momentous', use 'historic' (a HISTORIC agreement was signed). If you can substitute 'past-related' or 'concerning history', use 'historical' (HISTORICAL records show...). T4: examples -- The Battle of Hastings (1066) is a HISTORIC event (world-changing); a HISTORICAL novel is set in the past but the events may be made up; a HISTORIC building is one where something famous happened; a HISTORICAL building is just an old one. T5: the article rule -- both take 'a' in modern American English ('a historic moment', 'a historical event'); older writers sometimes wrote 'an historic' (with a silent H), which is fading but not wrong. Chicago accepts both.
source: Grokipedia 'Historic vs historical' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster 'historic' and 'historical' entries + extensive usage note; Chicago Manual of Style 17e 5.72 ('a/an historic' -- 'a' preferred), 5.250.
framing_note: REGISTER / CLARITY CONTRAST. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (HISTORY-MAKING vs HISTORY-RELATED). T5 gives the 'an historic' article-choice as a small style note. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the ambiguous use. DISTRACTOR MINE: economic/economical (same -ic/-ical pattern: economic = related to the economy, economical = thrifty), classic/classical. CHOICE PARITY. APOLITICAL: use Battle of Hastings (1066) or safe historic buildings, not current politics.

name: Comprise vs compose -- the whole includes the parts
scope: The rule that even careful writers get backwards. T1: 'The team is comprised of ten players' -- traditionally wrong. 'Comprise' means INCLUDE or CONTAIN, spoken by the WHOLE about its PARTS ('the team COMPRISES ten players' = the team contains ten players). 'Compose' means to MAKE UP, spoken by the PARTS about the WHOLE ('ten players COMPOSE the team' = they make up the team). T2: the memory trick -- the WHOLE COMPRISES its parts (whole first, comprise, parts); the PARTS COMPOSE the whole (parts first, compose, whole). Or: 'comprise' = 'contains'; 'compose' = 'make up'. T3: the swap tests -- 'the alphabet COMPRISES 26 letters' (contains 26); '26 letters COMPOSE the alphabet' (make up the alphabet). Both correct, different-direction. T4: the disputed form -- 'is comprised of' has been used for so long that dictionaries now list it, but most style guides (Chicago, AP, Garner's) still call it wrong; the alternative 'is composed of' is always correct. T5: the honest usage note -- 'comprised of' is now heard so often that stopping to correct it can seem pedantic; in casual speech, most listeners understand. In careful writing (essays, business, formal), stick with 'comprises' or 'is composed of'. Mark rung `vision_mandated: true` because this is a genuine live prescriptivist-vs-descriptivist call.
source: Grokipedia 'Comprise' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster 'comprise' extensive usage note (traces the 'comprised of' controversy back to the 1800s); Chicago Manual of Style 17e 5.250 ('comprised of' -- avoid); Garner's Modern English Usage 4e 'comprise' (Stage 4 for 'comprised of').
framing_note: PUNCHLINE-VIA-MISUSE + descriptivist question. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (whole/parts directionality). T5 crosses into descriptivist territory -- mark that rung `vision_mandated: true`. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the misuse. DISTRACTOR MINE: consist of, include, make up (all near-synonyms with slightly different directions). CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE: teams, alphabet, groups.

name: I before E except after C -- the rule and its exceptions
scope: The most-quoted spelling rule in English, and the honest exceptions. T1: is it 'recieve' or 'receive'? The classic rhyme -- 'I before E except after C' -- says receive (I comes AFTER the C = wrong; so it's E-I after C: reCEIve). Compare: beLIEve (no C before it, so I-E: I before E). T2: the pattern the rhyme covers -- I-E for most words (believe, achieve, piece, thief); E-I after C (receive, deceive, perceive, ceiling). T3: 'when the sound is AY' -- the fuller version of the rhyme adds 'or when sounded as AY, as in neighbor and weigh'. So EIGHT, WEIGHT, VEIN, REIN, SLEIGH, BEIGE all take E-I because they say AY. T4: the exceptions the rhyme MISSES -- 'weird', 'seize', 'either', 'neither', 'foreign', 'height', 'protein', 'caffeine', 'science', 'ancient' all break the rule. So many exceptions exist that linguists sometimes joke the rule 'has more counterexamples than examples'. T5: the honest teaching -- use the rhyme for the common words (receive, believe, deceive, achieve, piece, niece) where it works; MEMORIZE the exceptions (weird, seize, height, protein) because no rule catches them all. Spelling patterns in English are guides, not laws.
source: Grokipedia 'I before E except after C' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster 'ie/ei' spelling note; Oxford Dictionaries usage note on 'i before e' rule with the standard exception list.
framing_note: SPELLING-IN-USAGE-CONTEXT (grammar's edge -- spelling drills are OUT per subject config, but this rhyme is grammar-canon). Dinner-test payoff: T4 (the list of exceptions is longer than the list of rule-followers). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem quotes the misspelling or asks which follows the rule. DISTRACTOR MINE: other spelling rules (silent E lengthens the vowel, double consonant before -ing). CHOICE PARITY. KID-SAFE: school spelling contexts.

name: Common misspellings -- separate, definitely, accommodate
scope: The words even good spellers double-check. T1: 'seperate' -- wrong; the correct spelling is SEPARATE, with an A in the middle, not an E. The memory trick: separate has 'A RAT' in the middle -- sepARATe. T2: 'definately' or 'definitly' -- wrong; the correct spelling is DEFINITELY, with the FINITE word inside it (deFINITEly). Memory trick: it's DEFINITE plus -LY. T3: 'accomodate' or 'acommodate' -- wrong; the correct spelling is ACCOMMODATE, with DOUBLE C AND DOUBLE M. Memory trick: it accommodates two Cs and two Ms; the word is big enough to hold everyone. T4: 'embarass' -- wrong; the correct spelling is EMBARRASS, with DOUBLE R AND DOUBLE S. Memory trick: it's so embarrassing it has TWO Rs (to be REALLY, REALLY embarrassed) and TWO Ss. T5: other high-frequency traps -- 'occurred' (double C, double R -- unlike 'occur'); 'millennium' (double L, double N -- from Latin 'mille' + 'annus'); 'necessary' (one C, two Ss -- try 'one Collar, two Sleeves' as a mnemonic); 'occasionally' (double C, single S, double L); 'privilege' (no D anywhere -- it's LEG at the end, not LEDG).
source: Grokipedia 'Commonly misspelled English words' (browser lookup at build time); Merriam-Webster entries for each word; Oxford Dictionaries 'most commonly misspelled words' usage lists.
framing_note: SPELLING-IN-USAGE-CONTEXT with mnemonics. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (accommodate accommodates two Cs and two Ms) + T4 (embarrassing enough for two Rs and two Ss). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem shows the misspelling in a sentence and asks for the correct form. DISTRACTOR MINE: other plausible misspellings of each word (privileGE vs priviledGE; occurr vs ocurred). CHOICE PARITY: all four choices are plausible spellings of the target word. KID-SAFE: general vocabulary, school essays.

name: British vs American spelling -- colour, theatre, gray
scope: Two standard spellings, one language, both correct in their region. T1: 'color' vs 'colour' -- both correct. American English drops the U (color, honor, favor, labor); British English keeps it (colour, honour, favour, labour). Neither is 'wrong'; each is standard for its region. T2: 'theater' vs 'theatre' -- both correct. American English uses -ER (theater, center, meter, liter); British English uses -RE (theatre, centre, metre, litre). The one exception in American: 'acre' still ends in -RE. T3: 'gray' vs 'grey' -- both correct. American English usually GRAY, British English usually GREY. There's no rule; the E-vs-A is regional preference. T4: the -IZE / -ISE split -- American always uses -IZE (organize, realize, apologize); British often uses -ISE (organise, realise, apologise), though Oxford University Press actually prefers -IZE in British English too. T5: the pick-a-lane rule -- the important thing in a single piece of writing is CONSISTENCY: don't mix British and American in one document. If you're writing 'colour', also write 'theatre' and 'organise'; if you're writing 'color', also write 'theater' and 'organize'. Style guides call this ORTHOGRAPHIC CONSISTENCY. Neither system is right, but mixing them looks careless.
